claim: The 2-min/60-s timeout thresholds are hardcoded module constants with no configuration/experiment kill-switch, so they can't be tuned or disabled remotely.
raw: No configuration/experiment kill-switch for the timeout values — fetcherService.ts:303-310. The 2-min/60-s thresholds are hardcoded module constants shipped to all users at once... If 60 s turns out to be too aggressive... there is no way to tune or disable it without a code change and redeploy.

claim: The 60 s idle window may false-positive and abort a healthy request if a provider goes genuinely silent for >60 s during legitimate processing without heartbeats.
raw: 60 s idle window may false-positive on legitimately slow streams — fetcherService.ts:310, 354. ...this is safe as long as the server emits heartbeats/ping SSE comments during long server-side work... If a provider goes genuinely silent for >60 s during legitimate processing, this will abort a healthy request.

claim: StreamIdleTimeoutError surfaces incidentally as a generic NetworkError with the fetcher's generic user message; no dedicated user-facing message or explicit tested retry treatment. processError should handle it explicitly.
raw: The timeout surfaces as a generic error, not a recognized timeout — StreamIdleTimeoutError is a plain Error with a custom name... it lands as a NetworkError with the fetcher's generic user message; the gap is that there is no dedicated user-facing message... Consider handling StreamIdleTimeoutError explicitly in processError.

claim: Timeout destroy() calls reader.cancel() with no reason, so telemetry reports outcome:'cancel', making a hung-stream timeout indistinguishable from a user cancellation.
raw: Timeout is telemetered as a plain cancel — fetcherService.ts:104-107. destroy() calls reader.cancel() with no reason, so the counting stream's cancel transformer sees reason === undefined and reports outcome: 'cancel', indistinguishable from a user cancellation.

claim: There is no overall cap on total stream duration; because the idle timer resets on every chunk, a server dribbling one byte every 59 s streams forever.
raw: No overall cap on stream duration. Idle-timeout by design resets on every chunk, so a server dribbling one byte every 59 s streams forever. This matches the stated requirement... but if unbounded total time is a concern it isn't addressed.

claim: Tests are unit-only and never assert the stream is actually destroyed on timeout, that a real read() rejection propagates unchanged, or that the error propagates through processResponseFromChatEndpoint/SSEProcessor to a ChatFetchResponseType.
raw: Test gaps (unit-only). The tests never assert that (a) the underlying stream is actually destroyed/canceled on timeout, (b) a genuine mid-stream read() rejection propagates unchanged rather than being masked as a timeout, or (c) the error propagates through processResponseFromChatEndpoint/SSEProcessor to a ChatFetchResponseType.
